title: Declaring Beans with Annotations
description: Use @Component, @Service, @Repository to let Spring discover your classes.

slides.title: Spring’s Stereotype Annotations 🏷️
slides.content:
# Make Your Classes Beans

Spring can automatically detect and register your classes as beans if you annotate them with one of these stereotypes:

* **`@Component`** – Generic stereotype for any Spring‑managed bean.
* **`@Service`** – Indicates a service layer bean (business logic).
* **`@Repository`** – Indicates a DAO (Data Access Object) bean; adds persistence exception translation.
* **`@Controller`** – Already seen for web layer.

All of these are meta‑annotated with `@Component`, so Spring treats them the same – but they give hints about the class’s role.

quizData.question: Which annotation is best suited for a class that contains business logic?
quizData.explanation: `@Service` is a specialization of `@Component` that indicates a service layer class, making the intent clear.

slides.title: Component Scanning 🔍
slides.content:
# How Spring Finds Your Beans

Spring Boot automatically scans packages starting from the package of your `@SpringBootApplication` class. That’s why we put our service in `com.example.demo` – it’s inside the scan path.

You can also specify custom scan packages with `@ComponentScan`. But in most Spring Boot apps, you don’t need to – the default works perfectly.

slides.title: Bean Names 🔤
slides.content: By default, Spring uses the class name with the first letter lowercase as the bean name. So `GreetingService` becomes `greetingService`. You can change it by providing a name in the annotation: `@Service("customName")`.
